```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(pdmS7)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  error = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 3.6, dpi = if (nzchar(Sys.getenv("IN_PKGDOWN"))) 110 else 60, echo = FALSE
)
source("diagram.R")
pal <- c("#236b83", "#a26421", "#5b8c3a", "#8a3b6b", "#444444", "#b23b3b", "#9aa7b0")
```

The Probability Distributed Model, or PDM, turns rainfall into river flow. It was developed
by Bob Moore at the Institute of Hydrology and is widely used for flood forecasting in the
UK. This article explains how it works in plain terms, one idea at a time, with pictures of
the model running. The equations are in an appendix at the end, and in full on the
[Model equations](model-equations.html) page.

# The idea in one picture

```{r diagram, fig.height=5.2, fig.cap="The path water takes through the model."}
draw_process("pdm")
```

Rain falls on the soil. Some evaporates. Some soaks in and slowly drains down to
groundwater. Where the soil is already full, the rain cannot soak in and runs off quickly
over or near the surface. The quick water reaches the river within hours; the groundwater
seeps out over days and weeks. The river flow is the sum of the two.

Everything else in the model is detail about *how much* goes each way, and *how fast*.

# A catchment is many buckets of different sizes

The soil in a real catchment is not the same everywhere. A thin soil on a hilltop fills
with a few millimetres of rain; a deep soil in a valley can hold a hundred. The PDM does not
try to map where each soil is. Instead it imagines the catchment as a great many small
buckets of different sizes, and describes only how many buckets there are of each size.

```{r buckets, fig.height=3.4, fig.cap="Thirty buckets standing for a catchment's soils, sorted by size. Rain fills them all to the same level; the dark buckets are full, so any more rain on them runs off. Left: after a little rain. Right: after a lot."}
soil <- FlodeParetoCapacity(cmin = 0, cmax = 150, b = 0.4)
sizes <- sort(150 * (1 - (1 - (seq_len(30) - 0.5) / 30)^(1 / 0.4)))
draw_buckets <- function(level, title) {
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0.5, 30.5), ylim = c(0, 160), xaxt = "n", xlab = "", main = title,
       ylab = "Bucket size (mm of water)", cex.main = 0.9)
  full <- sizes <= level
  rect(seq_len(30) - 0.4, 0, seq_len(30) + 0.4, sizes, border = pal[5], col = "white")
  rect(seq_len(30) - 0.4, 0, seq_len(30) + 0.4, pmin(sizes, level), border = NA,
       col = ifelse(full, pal[1], grDevices::adjustcolor(pal[1], 0.35)))
  abline(h = level, lty = 2, col = pal[2])
  mtext(sprintf("%d of 30 full", sum(full)), side = 1, line = 0.5, cex = 0.8)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(2, 4.2, 2, 0.6))
draw_buckets(25, "After a little rain")
draw_buckets(80, "After a lot of rain")
```

Two things follow from this simple picture:

- **The same storm does different things on dry and wet ground.** When the soil is dry, few
  buckets are full and most rain soaks in. When it is wet, many are full and much of the rain
  runs straight off.
- **The share of ground that is "full" grows during a storm.** The model calls this the
  *saturated fraction*: the share of the catchment where new rain runs off.

Three numbers describe the buckets: the size of the largest (`cmax`), the size of the
smallest (`cmin`, usually zero), and the shape `b`, which says whether most buckets are small
or most are large. The Pareto distribution shown here is the standard choice; four others
are described in [Choosing model components](model-options.html).

# The same storm on dry and wet ground

Here one storm, 20 mm over six hours, falls on the same catchment three times: once when the
soil is 20 per cent full, once at half full, and once at 85 per cent full.

```{r dry-wet, fig.cap="The same 20 mm storm (shaded) on dry, middling and wet soil. The wetter the soil, the more of the storm runs off and the higher the flood."}
config <- pdm_presets("standard")
config$area_km2 <- 40
config$recharge$kg <- 300
config$distribution$cmax <- 150
model <- pdm_from_config(config)
storm <- data.frame(rain = c(rep(0, 6), rep(20 / 6, 6), rep(0, 24)), pet = 0.05)
wetness <- c(0.2, 0.5, 0.85)
runs <- lapply(wetness, function(w) run_pdm(model, storm, initial_state(model, w))$output)
par(mar = c(4, 4.2, 0.6, 0.6))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 36), ylim = c(0, max(sapply(runs, function(o) max(o$q_m3s)))),
     xlab = "Hour", ylab = "River flow (m3/s)")
rect(6, -1, 12, 100, col = grDevices::adjustcolor(pal[7], 0.2), border = NA)
for (i in seq_along(runs)) lines(seq_len(36), runs[[i]]$q_m3s, lwd = 2, col = pal[i])
legend("topright", paste0("soil ", 100 * wetness, "% full: ",
                          round(sapply(runs, function(o) sum(o$direct_runoff_mm)), 1),
                          " mm runs off"), col = pal[1:3], lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

On dry ground under 2 mm of the 20 runs off; on wet ground over a third does. This is the
heart of the PDM, and why the state of the soil before a storm matters so much to a flood
forecast.

# Through a wet spell

Over two months of showers and storms, the soil wets up and dries out, and the saturated
fraction rises and falls with it.

```{r season-data}
set.seed(4)
n <- 24 * 60
time <- seq(as.POSIXct("2024-01-01", tz = "UTC"), by = 3600, length.out = n)
forcing <- data.frame(time = time, pet = 0.08,
                      rain = ifelse(stats::runif(n) < 0.05, stats::rgamma(n, 0.8, scale = 4), 0))
forcing$rain[24 * 20 + seq_len(24 * 8)] <- 0
start <- initial_state_from_flow(model, 0.6, 0.7)
season <- run_pdm(model, forcing, start)$output
```

```{r season, fig.height=6.2, fig.cap="Two months of hourly rain (top), the water in the soil (middle) and the saturated fraction (bottom). Rain wets the soil and spreads the saturated area; dry days let evaporation and drainage pull both back down."}
par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(1.5, 4.5, 0.6, 0.6), oma = c(2.5, 0, 0, 0))
plot(time, forcing$rain, type = "h", col = pal[1], xaxt = "n", xlab = "",
     ylab = "Rain (mm/h)")
plot(time, season$soil_mm, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = pal[3], xaxt = "n", xlab = "",
     ylab = "Soil water (mm)")
plot(time, 100 * season$saturated_fraction, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = pal[2], xlab = "",
     ylab = "Saturated (%)")
```

Between storms the soil loses water two ways: **evaporation**, which takes more when the soil
is wetter, and **drainage** down to groundwater (called *recharge*), which also runs faster
when the soil is fuller. Both are why the curves sag through the long dry spell in late
January, and recover quickly when rain returns.

# Two paths to the river

Water that runs off goes through a **fast store**: in the standard model, two small
reservoirs one after the other, which smooth and delay the runoff by a few hours. Water that
drains to groundwater goes through a **slow store**, which releases it over days and weeks.
The river flow is the two added together.

```{r paths, fig.cap="River flow split into its two parts. The quick surface part makes the peaks; the slow groundwater part makes the steady flow between them and the long recession."}
area <- config$area_km2
fast <- season$surface_out_mm * area / 3.6
slow <- season$baseflow_out_mm * area / 3.6
par(mar = c(3, 4.2, 0.6, 0.6))
plot(time, fast + slow, type = "n", xlab = "", ylab = "River flow (m3/s)")
polygon(c(time, rev(time)), c(slow, rep(0, n)), col = grDevices::adjustcolor(pal[3], 0.5),
        border = NA)
polygon(c(time, rev(time)), c(fast + slow, rev(slow)), col = grDevices::adjustcolor(pal[1], 0.6),
        border = NA)
legend("topleft", c("fast (surface) flow", "slow (groundwater) flow"),
       fill = c(grDevices::adjustcolor(pal[1], 0.6), grDevices::adjustcolor(pal[3], 0.5)),
       border = NA, bty = "n")
```

How fast each store empties is set by its *time constant*: how long, roughly, water stays in
it. The fast stores have time constants of hours (`k1`, `k2`); the groundwater store's
constant (`kb`) is much longer.

# Where the water went

Over the two months, every millimetre of rain is accounted for:

```{r balance, fig.height=2.4, fig.cap="Where the two months' rain went, in millimetres over the catchment."}
gone <- c(Evaporation = sum(season$aet_mm), `Fast flow` = sum(season$surface_out_mm),
          `Slow flow` = sum(season$baseflow_out_mm))
gone <- c(gone, Stored = sum(season$rain_corrected_mm) - sum(gone))
par(mar = c(4, 1, 0.6, 1))
mid <- barplot(as.matrix(gone), horiz = TRUE, col = pal[c(2, 1, 3, 7)], border = "white",
               xlab = paste0("mm (rain: ", round(sum(season$rain_corrected_mm)), " mm)"))
ends <- cumsum(gone)
text(ends - gone / 2, mid, paste0(names(gone), "\n", round(gone), " mm"), col = "white",
     cex = 0.75, font = 2)
round(c(Rain = sum(season$rain_corrected_mm), gone), 1)
```

What is not evaporated or carried to the river stays in the stores. pdmS7 checks this
balance at every time step; it closes to rounding error.

# What each setting does

Calibrating a PDM by hand means knowing which setting changes which part of the hydrograph.
Each panel below changes one setting, holding the others fixed, over the same week of the
wet spell.

```{r knobs, fig.height=7.5, fig.cap="One week of flow as each setting is lowered (light), left at its value (dark) and raised (orange)."}
window <- 24 * 33 + seq_len(24 * 7)
knobs <- list(
  list(path = "fc", label = "fc: rainfall factor", values = c(0.85, 1, 1.15)),
  list(path = "distribution.cmax", label = "cmax: largest bucket (mm)",
       values = c(90, 150, 250)),
  list(path = "distribution.b", label = "b: bucket shape", values = c(0.15, 0.4, 1.2)),
  list(path = "recharge.kg", label = "kg: drainage time constant (h)",
       values = c(100, 300, 900)),
  list(path = "surface.k1", label = "k1, k2: fast store time constants (h)",
       values = c(1, 2, 5)),
  list(path = "groundwater.kb", label = "kb: groundwater constant", values = c(3000, 10000, 30000))
)
set_value <- function(cfg, path, value) {
  keys <- strsplit(path, ".", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
  if (length(keys) == 1) cfg[[keys]] <- value else cfg[[keys[1]]][[keys[2]]] <- value
  cfg
}
simulate <- function(cfg) {
  m <- pdm_from_config(cfg)
  run_pdm(m, forcing, initial_state_from_flow(m, 0.6, 0.7))$output$q_m3s[window]
}
par(mfrow = c(3, 2), mar = c(2, 4.2, 1.6, 0.6))
for (k in knobs) {
  flows <- lapply(k$values, function(v) {
    cfg <- config
    cfg <- set_value(cfg, k$path, v)
    if (k$path == "surface.k1") cfg$surface$k2 <- 2 * v
    simulate(cfg)
  })
  plot(NA, xlim = c(1, length(window)), ylim = c(0, max(unlist(flows))), xaxt = "n",
       xlab = "", ylab = "m3/s", main = k$label, cex.main = 0.9)
  cols <- c(pal[7], pal[1], pal[2])
  for (i in 1:3) lines(flows[[i]], col = cols[i], lwd = c(1.5, 2, 1.5)[i])
}
```

| Setting | What it changes | Raise it when the model is... |
|---|---|---|
| `fc` | All rain, before anything else. The whole hydrograph scales with it | Too dry overall |
| `cmax` | How much the soil can hold. Larger means less runoff and more evaporation | Too flashy, peaks too high |
| `b` | Whether the catchment has mostly large or mostly small buckets. Larger `b` means more small buckets, so more runoff and higher peaks | Peaks too low for the size of the storms |
| `kg` | How slowly soil drains to groundwater. Larger means more surface runoff, less baseflow | Peaks too low and baseflow too high |
| `k1`, `k2` | How quickly runoff reaches the river. Larger means later, lower, broader peaks | Peaks too early or too sharp |
| `kb` | How slowly groundwater empties. Larger means flatter, longer recessions | Recessions too steep |
| `td` | A pure delay before water reaches the outlet | Everything is early by a fixed time |

The [scorecard](scoring.html) points to the right setting: a volume error suggests `fc`,
peaks too small suggest the fast stores or `kg`, and a poor low-flow score suggests `kb`.

# The equations, briefly

In this appendix, depths are millimetres over the catchment and $\Delta t$ is the time
step in hours. The full set, with Moore's (2007) equation numbers and every detail of the
implementation, is on the [Model equations](model-equations.html) page.

**Buckets.** If $F(c)$ is the share of the catchment whose bucket holds no more than $c$ mm,
and every bucket is filled to the same level $C$, the soil water averaged over the catchment
is

$$s(C)=\int_0^C [1-F(c)]\,dc.$$

For the Pareto distribution, $F(c)=1-(1-c/c_{\max})^b$, and the saturated fraction is $F(C)$.

**Evaporation.** Actual evaporation is the potential rate $e_p$ reduced as the soil dries,
with $s_{\max}$ the mean bucket size:

$$e=e_p\left[1-\left(1-s/s_{\max}\right)^{b_e}\right].$$

**Drainage to groundwater.** Above a threshold $s_t$ (usually zero),

$$d=\frac{(s-s_t)^{b_g}}{k_g}\Delta t.$$

**Runoff.** Rain left after evaporation and drainage raises the filling level; whatever
cannot be stored runs off:

$$v=n-\left[s(C+n)-s(C)\right].$$

**Routing.** Each store empties at a rate set by how much it holds: $dX/dt=u-q(X)$, with
$q=X/k$ for a linear store and $q=X^3/k_b$ for the standard cubic groundwater store.

**Flow.** The routed depths become flow in m³/s through the catchment area $A$ in km²:
$Q=\frac{A}{3.6}\,\frac{V_{\mathrm{fast}}+V_{\mathrm{slow}}}{\Delta t}$.
